1: Good morning. Thank you, Mister President and members of the jury, for the time you give me today. My name is Mouad Louhichi. My thesis is titled Cooperative Game Theory for Explainable AI in Recommendation Systems: A Shapley Framework for Actionable Insight, supervised by Professor Mohamed Lazaar. It defends one idea: Shapley attribution is not only a post-hoc explanation. It can explain black-box clustering, stay consistent across levels, and finally guide what a recommender learns.
2: The talk has seven parts: introduction, context and problem, the shared protocol, the three contributions, and the conclusion. Each contribution follows the same order: gap, objectives, method, protocol, results, findings. The small squares at the top right show where we are. Backup tables are placed after the end, for questions.
3: Let me start with the introduction: why explainability is a core requirement for recommender systems, and what I mean by an actionable insight. Time check: minute 1.
4: Three questions frame the work. Everywhere: black-box models shape what billions of people see, buy and watch. The black box: even strong recommenders and clustering pipelines are hard to question; we see the output, not the reason. Trust: transparency should be built into the model, not added after the fact. As models gain power, they lose transparency. I treat accuracy and interpretability as two goals to meet together.
5: The whole thesis is framed around actionable insight. An explanation is actionable when it points to a factor that can be changed, when that change leads to a clear change in the output, and when the factor is stated in the domain's own terms: a chemical variable, a pollution indicator, a preference signal. Never a hidden latent code. A good explanation supports a real decision.
6: The context is the move from simple to hypergraph recommenders. Matrix factorisation used latent factors with no readable meaning. Graph neural networks replaced the hidden code with a hidden message-passing mechanism. Hypergraph models added user-item-context relations, but assume that every message counts the same. Each step added power and removed transparency, while the EU AI Act, the OECD principles and the GDPR ask for meaningful explanation. So attribution should be part of the model itself.
7: Recommendation is infrastructure for everyday decisions. Streaming platforms decide what you watch, music services what you hear, e-commerce what you buy, social feeds what you read. Each system is accurate, and its reasoning is hidden. Everywhere, and hidden: that is what makes explainability a core requirement.
8: Now the problem itself. I go quickly over the four main approaches, then the limitations, the five research questions, and the three contributions. Time check: about minute 3.
ap_content: Four families of recommender, one slide each, because their limits motivate the thesis. First, content-based filtering: the system builds a profile of what the user liked, in terms of item features such as genre or brand, and recommends items whose features match. It is explainable by construction: the reason is a named feature. The limit: it needs good metadata and recommends more of the same. That level of explanation, domain factors, is the level I want to preserve.
ap_cf: Second, collaborative filtering. The system ignores item content and uses the behaviour of other users: users who agreed in the past will agree in the future. Here user one and user two share items one and two, so user two's interest in item three is passed to user one. It is the base of matrix factorisation and of graph recommenders. Its weakness: new users and items have no history, and sparse matrices give little signal.
ap_hybrid: Third, hybrid approaches and matrix factorisation. A hybrid mixes content and collaborative signals, which reduces cold-start. Matrix factorisation splits the interaction matrix R into two low-rank matrices, P for users and Q for items, with k latent factors. It is accurate, scalable, and still the standard baseline. But the factors are hidden: nobody can say what factor seven means. The field gained accuracy and lost the named explanation.
ap_graph: Fourth, graph and hypergraph recommenders, the state of the art. Users and items become nodes, interactions become edges, and message passing, as in LightGCN, HCCF or HPCF, moves information over several hops. A hyperedge can join a user, an item and a context at once, which gives the best accuracy on sparse benchmarks. The limit, in the orange box: these models are costly and treat all messages as equally important. Contribution III challenges exactly that.
10: Four classical limitations. Sparsity and scalability: the matrix is almost empty. Cold-start: no history for a new user or item. Popularity bias and the filter-bubble loop. And the one this thesis targets: the lack of interpretability. For clustering it is even harder: methods give a local or a global explanation, not both; they struggle to scale; and they rarely stay consistent across levels of detail. That is the gap I work on.
11: Three problems. Lack of explainability: complex models are hard to explain in a faithful and actionable way. Difficulty of scaling: local explanations do not carry over to multi-level structures or large data. Weak link with learning: explanations are post-hoc and never shape how the model learns. So the literature lacks one cooperative-attribution framework that explains clustering faithfully, stays consistent across levels, and works as an in-training signal. My claim is that Shapley attribution can be that framework.
12: The aim: develop, justify and evaluate a cooperative-game view of explainable AI for clustering and recommendation. Five research questions. RQ1: how can Shapley values explain black-box clustering faithfully? RQ2: how does that extend to large-scale, multi-level clustering while staying feasible and consistent? RQ3: can cooperative attribution become part of how a recommender learns? RQ4: can it improve accuracy, context and diversity at the same time? RQ5, the thesis-level question: what do we gain when both tasks are read as one shared view?
13: Three contributions, one thread. C1: Shapley-based explanation of black-box clustering with a PCA, K-Means, LightGBM, TreeSHAP pipeline, on wine quality. C2: the same logic scaled to multi-level, large data with cross-level SHAP aggregation, on Beijing air quality. C3, the strongest claim: DyHuCoG turns the attribution into an in-training signal inside a hypergraph recommender, on MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Book. One argument that builds step by step.
14: In one view: the thesis is a single claim. Shapley attribution can work as one shared, explainable view across clustering and recommendation. Each contribution applies the same cooperative-game logic at a different stage, from explaining a partition to guiding what a recommender learns. Explanation becomes part of the model.
15: Before the contributions, the shared experimental setup, so that the comparisons are clearly fair: datasets, splitting, baselines, metrics and hardware. Time check: about minute 8.
16: Two clustering datasets and two recommendation datasets. For clustering I chose data whose features have a clear meaning, because the method returns attribution to the original variables: Wine Quality, small and dense, and Beijing Air Quality, large and noisy. For recommendation, two standard benchmarks with a strong density contrast: MovieLens-1M at 0.0447 and Amazon-Book at 0.0006. That contrast tests whether Shapley guidance helps most when interaction data are weak.
ds_wine: First, Portuguese white wines from the UCI repository: four thousand eight hundred and ninety-eight samples and eleven laboratory measurements, acidity, sugar, sulfur dioxide, density, pH, alcohol. Every column has a physical meaning, so when the explanation says density and pH, a wine maker knows what to do.
ds_beijing: Second, Beijing Multi-Site Air Quality: three hundred and eighty-three thousand hourly records from 2013 to 2017, six pollutants and five weather variables. Large, noisy and seasonal, it is the stress test for Contribution II. Pollutants and weather sit side by side, so the explanation can show that the weather sets the regime.
ds_ml1m: Third, MovieLens-1M: about one million ratings from six thousand and forty users on three thousand seven hundred movies. Ratings above three become positive feedback and genre is the context proxy. It is the standard benchmark, so the numbers stay comparable with LightGCN, HCCF and HPCF.
ds_amazon: Fourth, Amazon-Book: fifty-two thousand users, ninety-one thousand books, three million interactions, and a density of six in ten thousand. A review is an interaction and the category is the context. It tests whether Shapley weighting helps most when the signal is weakest.
18: Splitting is designed against leakage. Clustering uses five-fold cross-validation for the surrogate and the attribution. Recommendation uses a user-level, time-ordered split, seventy, ten, twenty, with the latest test positive per user as the leave-one-out target and popularity-aware negatives. Five seeds, early stopping on validation NDCG at twenty.
19: The baselines. For clustering, a LIME-based surrogate, the standard alternative to SHAP. For recommendation, six baselines from four families: matrix factorisation with BPR, NCF, LightGCN, RecDCL, and the hypergraph models HCCF and HPCF, with HPCF from 2025 as the strongest reference. I claim superiority only against the models tested here.
metrics: The metrics with their formulas. NDCG at K, the headline, rewards relevant items placed near the top. Recall and Precision at K. Two beyond-accuracy measures: catalogue coverage, the fraction of the catalogue ever recommended, and intra-list diversity, the average dissimilarity inside one list; ILD is built into the DyHuCoG utility, not only reported. For clustering, the Silhouette and Davies-Bouldin; the Silhouette is also the value function of the clustering game.
20: Hardware, because it explains the runtime figures later: an Intel Core i9 for clustering and one NVIDIA RTX 4090 for DyHuCoG, with scikit-learn, LightGBM, SHAP and PyTorch. Standard academic hardware.
21: Contribution I: explaining black-box clustering with Shapley values. It answers RQ1. I present the gap and the objectives, then a short technical deep dive into cooperative games and the Shapley value, then method, protocol, results and findings. Time check: about minute 11.
22: Why start with clustering? The model creates its own structure, so the meaning of a cluster must be worked out after the fact: the hardest test bed for attribution. The gap: methods give a local or a global explanation, rarely both; they often fail to scale; and they rarely stay consistent across clusters. Local surrogates such as LIME describe one point, with no guarantee that the credit is fair or stable. There is no axiomatic way to explain a black-box partition in the original feature space.
23: RQ1 breaks into three objectives. O1: a cluster-level explanation that keeps feature-level attribution. O2: attribution in the original feature space, because that is what makes it actionable. O3: justify why Shapley is the right allocation rule rather than an ad-hoc surrogate such as LIME.
dd_game: Three slides for the one mathematical object the thesis rests on. A cooperative game has three ingredients: a set of players N; coalitions, any subset S, two to the power n of them; and a characteristic function v that gives each coalition the value it creates alone, with the empty coalition worth zero. The question is one of fairness: the grand coalition earns v of N; how should it be shared? Take a three-piece band. Guitar, Voice and Drums alone earn sixty, forty and twenty. Guitar and Voice together earn one hundred and forty, more than the sum; the whole band earns two hundred. Because of this synergy, a fair split must credit what a player adds to the others.
dd_shapley: Shapley's answer, from 1953: let the players arrive one at a time in a random order, and pay each one what they add at the moment they arrive. With three players there are six orders. Take Voice, Drums, Guitar: Voice creates forty; Drums makes the pair worth eighty, so adds forty; Guitar completes the band, eighty becomes two hundred, so adds one hundred and twenty. Averaging over the six orders gives ninety, seventy and forty, and that sums exactly to two hundred. The formula on the right is the same computation in general: a weighted sum over all coalitions without j of the marginal contribution of j. The four axioms, efficiency, symmetry, null player and additivity, are why this is the right rule: Shapley proved it is the only rule that satisfies all four.
dd_thesis: The same game appears three times in the thesis. In Contribution I the players are the eleven wine features and the value of a coalition is the Silhouette of K-Means run with only those features. In Contribution II the players are the same, but the game is played at each level of the hierarchy. In Contribution III the players are users, items and contexts, and the value is the utility of the recommendation they produce together: accuracy, diversity and novelty, estimated by Monte Carlo with fifty permutations. The crucial difference is the last row: in the first two chapters the Shapley value explains a model after training; in the third it is used during training. The axioms never change.
24: So, clustering as a cooperative game: the features are the players, and the value of coalition S is the Silhouette of K-Means run on the feature subset X sub S, with a fixed k. A feature gets a high Shapley value when adding it improves separation, on average over all coalitions. But there are two to the power of the number of features coalitions, so we need a bridge to a practical computation.
25: The bridge is the heart of the method. TreeSHAP explains tree models, not K-Means centroids, and explaining the PCA space would move attribution away from the variables we care about. So we turn the partition into a supervised task: K-Means gives cluster labels, a LightGBM classifier learns to predict them from the original features, and TreeSHAP explains that surrogate, exactly. Attribution stays in the original space. The validity condition is surrogate fidelity: macro-F1 of about 0.82 is the floor.
26: Five stages. Standardisation. PCA, used only as a computational and visual check, never as the explanatory space. K-Means plus-plus with a multi-criteria choice of k. The LightGBM surrogate on the original features. And TreeSHAP attribution, aggregated into global importance, cluster profiles and local force plots. TreeSHAP scales with tree count and depth, not exponentially in the number of features.
c1_protocol: The protocol. Wine Quality, eleven standardised features. K-Means plus-plus with k from two to ten, chosen by elbow, Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin and an interpretability check. A LightGBM surrogate with five-fold cross-validation; macro-F1 is the fidelity score. Exact TreeSHAP in the original space, and a LIME surrogate on the same partition as the comparison point. Success: fidelity floor met, chemically meaningful ranking, distinct cluster signatures.
27: An honest point. I evaluate k from two to ten and select three on purpose, although it is not the best geometry: with two clusters the Silhouette is 0.214, with three it is 0.144. I choose three because three clusters support three distinct, chemically meaningful wine stories, which is far more actionable. And to avoid a confusion: the 0.63 Silhouette belongs to Beijing in Contribution II, not to wine.
28: The global SHAP ranking is led by density, then pH, fixed acidity, the sulfur dioxide variables and alcohol. These are exactly the variables a wine expert would point to for structure, preservation and balance. This is not a side effect of the classifier: the surrogate reproduces the partition from the original variables, and TreeSHAP attributes in that space, so the pipeline recovers domain knowledge without being told.
29: The cluster profiles show that each cluster has its own signature. Cluster zero is driven by density and the sulfur dioxide variables; cluster one by acidity and pH; cluster two by a different balance of acidity, alcohol and related attributes. The same small set of variables returns in all three, with different weights. A cluster is not just a label; it is a distinct, domain-meaningful combination of drivers.
30: Why Shapley rather than LIME. SHAP satisfies four axioms: efficiency, symmetry, null player and additivity. LIME fits a local surrogate with no such guarantee and is sensitive to the perturbation design. SHAP gives local and global explanations and can compare clusters; LIME cannot. One caveat: here efficiency holds with respect to the LightGBM output, not directly to the Silhouette game, which is why surrogate fidelity matters.
31: The answer to RQ1 is yes. Shapley values explain a black-box partition faithfully, provided the surrogate has high fidelity, and consistently at cluster level. O1 is met: a global and a per-cluster reading. O2 is met: attribution returns to the original chemical variables. O3 is met: Shapley satisfies the four axioms and LIME does not. The caveat stands: efficiency holds with respect to the surrogate output.
32: The findings in short: the partition is explained at cluster and instance level, in the original variables, with a chemically meaningful ranking and an axiomatic basis that LIME lacks.
33: The limits. The explanation depends on surrogate fidelity; it is not a direct mechanism of the K-Means geometry. It is limited to tabular data. It is single-level: it cannot yet say how feature importance changes between a partition and its sub-partitions. And representative-instance reporting smooths out some variation. These limits start Contribution II.
34: The takeaway: Shapley attribution is one well-founded lens for explaining an unsupervised partition, and keeping it in the original feature space is what makes it actionable. But real data are rarely single-level. Can the same logic scale to multi-level, large-scale clustering without losing consistency? That is Contribution II.
35: Contribution II: scaling the explanation to multi-level, large-scale clustering. It answers RQ2, and the concern is not only scale but several levels of detail. Time check: about minute 20.
36: The gap. Once clustering is multi-level, feature importance must stay readable within a cluster, across sub-clusters and across levels. Three hundred and eighty-three thousand records cannot be explained coalition by coalition. A flat explanation may be true yet incomplete. And hierarchical clustering work gives no formal link between a parent's explanation and its children's.
37: RQ2 asks how the Shapley explanation extends to large-scale, multi-level clustering while staying feasible and consistent. Three objectives. O1: a truly multi-level workflow with level-specific surrogates. O2: a formal cross-level consistency argument, Proposition 6.1. O3: validation at scale on data far from wine, the Beijing air-quality records.
38: The workflow is recursive: a coarse clustering on the full dataset, then each cluster split again where it makes sense. Each level gets its own surrogate and SHAP values in the same original space. The aggregation is not a naive average: a parent-level attribution is a size-weighted expectation over its children. One point of method: the hierarchy is an analysis tool, not a claim that the data have a true natural hierarchy.
39: Proposition 6.1 is the mathematical heart. Let Phi at level l, cluster c, feature j, be the expected absolute SHAP importance in that cluster, and w sub c prime the relative size of a child. For a strict nested hierarchy on a consistent feature space, the parent's importance equals the size-weighted sum of its children's importance, plus a residual epsilon from surrogate mismatch that vanishes under perfect fidelity. The proof uses the law of total expectation. It does not say explanations are identical across levels; it says their differences can be interpreted, not ruled out as inconsistency.
c2_protocol: Same template. Beijing, three hundred and eighty-three thousand records, eleven variables. Level one: K-Means plus-plus on the full data. Level two: each coarse cluster split again, three regimes into nine sub-clusters. One LightGBM surrogate and exact TreeSHAP per level, aggregation by Proposition 6.1, and a sensitivity analysis over k, projection dimension and surrogate depth.
40: On Beijing the k-selection criteria agree strongly. The full dataset clusters cleanly into three, with a Silhouette of about 0.63 and a Davies-Bouldin of about 0.55, so the clusters rarely overlap. This is where the 0.63 comes from: Beijing, not wine. The two-component PCA view is for inspection only. The conclusions are robust to small changes in k, in projection dimension and in surrogate depth; only low-ranked variables shift.
41: The global ranking is led by temperature, dew point and pressure, then carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide, PM10 and PM2.5. It is striking that the weather variables, not only the pollutants, dominate. Temperature, dew point and pressure control dispersion, trapping and sunlight-driven chemistry: they set the conditions under which pollution builds up. A naive ranking of concentrations would miss that the weather sets the regime.
42: The force plots reveal three regimes. Regime A is warm and sunlight-driven: ozone, temperature and dew point stand out, typical of summer photochemical smog. Regime B is winter smog: carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and particulate matter, with low wind limiting dispersion. Regime C is comparatively clean air with favourable weather. The value is in showing which combination of variables defines each regime, so an analyst can see the drivers of a given episode.
43: The main payoff. At the coarse level, temperature and dew point dominate, because they separate the broad regimes. Inside single clusters, the informative variables shift to carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, PM10, wind speed or ozone. This is not a contradiction; it is what a multi-level explanation should reveal. The parent-level story is regime selection; the cluster-level story is variation within a regime. Proposition 6.1 lets us read these shifts as structure, not noise.
44: The same logic works on a small, dense, chemically correlated dataset and on a large, noisy environmental one, which supports generality. Against the SHAP-based clustering literature, our Beijing partition reaches a Silhouette of about 0.63, where Gramegna and Giudici report about 0.37 on credit data. Against LIME, we see weaker cross-level consistency. These are comparative observations, not a full benchmark.
45: The answer to RQ2 is yes, within bounds. Shapley-based explanation scales to multi-level, large-scale settings without losing consistency, provided the hierarchy is modelled explicitly and the approximation is transparent. O1: a multi-level explanation that does not collapse into a flat summary. O2: Proposition 6.1 gives the formal consistency argument. O3: validation on Beijing. The bound is that this is still an explanation of a pre-computed partition.
46: In short: the explanation scales because the hierarchy is explicit, Proposition 6.1 makes cross-level differences interpretable, and the method generalises to a very different, large and noisy dataset.
47: The limitations. The clustering stays static although the Beijing data are temporal. Surrogate-based SHAP with representative instances smooths out variation between observations. The approach is limited to tabular data. And, most important, the attribution is still post-hoc: it never influences learning. That is the bridge to Contribution III.
48: The takeaway: Shapley attribution stays consistent across levels of detail once the hierarchy is explicit, so explanations become interpretable at scale. But it still explains a partition that was already computed. Can cooperative attribution move beyond explanation and become part of how a recommender learns? That is Contribution III.
49: The third and main contribution: DyHuCoG, a Dynamic Hypergraph Cooperative Game, where Shapley attribution becomes an in-training signal inside a hypergraph recommender. It answers RQ3 and RQ4. Time check: about minute 27.
50: The gap. Graph and hypergraph recommenders treat message importance as uniform or attention-weighted, with no principled account of how much each user, item or context adds. Diversity is handled by re-ranking after training. Interpretability is added after prediction. And my first two contributions were still post-hoc. So the gap is a recommender that uses a cooperative-game utility, during training, to decide how much each player counts.
51: RQ3: can cooperative attribution become part of how a recommender learns? RQ4: can it improve accuracy, context and diversity together? Three objectives. O1: formulate recommendation as a cooperative game over users, items and contexts, with a utility that mixes accuracy, diversity and novelty. O2: embed preference-aware Monte Carlo Shapley estimates into hypergraph message passing as dynamic hyperedge weights. O3: improve ranking, coverage and diversity together against the strongest baseline, on two datasets.
52: The game. Players are users, items and contexts. Hyperedges encode user-item-context interactions, with dynamic weights derived from Shapley estimates. A coalition is the set of entities taking part in a recommendation episode, and its value is the quality of the recommendation they achieve together. The task is top-N recommendation that balances relevance, diversity and contextual fit. This mirrors the clustering game on purpose: same logic, different value function.
53: The coalition utility is a weighted sum of NDCG at twenty, a diversity term and a context score. This is the same trade-off the recommender must satisfy, so the explanatory game and the predictive objective are aligned by design. A preference bonus adds the user-item similarities inside the coalition. Alpha, beta and gamma were grid-searched to 0.60, 0.25 and 0.15, with lambda at 0.20, and NDCG is stable within one and a half percent around that point.
54: Exact Shapley is not feasible here, so we use a Monte Carlo estimator: over M sampled coalitions, average the value with the player minus the value without. It is unbiased and its error falls as one over root M. We chose M equal to fifty: about ninety-nine percent accuracy. Because preferences change, the estimates are refreshed every ten batches and smoothed with an exponential moving average.
55: The architecture is the decisive move. Base propagation is standard hypergraph message passing. The Shapley-weighted version multiplies each message by a normalised Shapley coefficient, after clipping and smoothing. Layer fusion combines the layers, an attention gate blends the Shapley-weighted score with the standard score as a stabiliser, and a context term is added. The model is told not only who is connected to whom, but how much each coalition is worth, and that worth controls how information flows.
56: The loss has four terms: BPR for ranking, an intra-list diversity regulariser, a context loss that aligns the context embedding with the context node, and weight decay. Negatives come from a popularity-aware distribution with periodic hard-negative refresh; the optimiser is Adam. The point is alignment: the model optimises the same accuracy-diversity-context balance that the attribution is computed from, so the explanation is a read-out of the objective, faithful by design.
c3_protocol: The protocol. MovieLens-1M, dense, and Amazon-Book, sparse, with Yelp2018 as an extra check. Time-ordered split, six baselines with HPCF as the strongest, four metrics over five seeds. Paired t-tests and Wilcoxon on per-user NDCG with Holm-Bonferroni correction and Cohen's d. An ablation removes one component at a time. Success: beat HPCF on both datasets with corrected p below 0.05, coverage and diversity rising together, overhead within about two times HPCF.
57: The headline result on MovieLens-1M, DyHuCoG in bold, best on all four metrics. HPCF reaches an NDCG at twenty of 0.2528; DyHuCoG gives 0.2775, plus 9.8 percent, and recall goes from 0.2098 to 0.2362, plus 12.6 percent. At the same time coverage rises from 0.342 to 0.397 and diversity from 0.461 to 0.516. The gap widens from classical to graph to hypergraph, and DyHuCoG adds one more step. Standard deviations, in the backup, are about a tenth of the gap.
58: Same table for Amazon-Book, density six in ten thousand. Same picture, larger relative gains: plus 13.3 percent NDCG and plus 16.2 percent recall over HPCF, coverage up nearly thirty percent, diversity up 12.5 percent. Absolute values are low for every model because the matrix is almost empty; what matters is the consistent ordering and the wider gap where data are weakest.
c3_fig72: This thesis figure puts all seven models side by side, NDCG on the left, Recall on the right. Look at the shape: a monotone ladder. Matrix factorisation lowest, then NCF, then LightGCN, then the hypergraph models, and DyHuCoG the tallest bar in every panel, with a visibly larger gap on Amazon-Book. All models were tuned with the same budget and the same early-stopping rule.
59: Coverage and intra-list diversity for HPCF and DyHuCoG. Coverage is up sixteen percent on MovieLens-1M and thirty percent on Amazon-Book; diversity is up twelve percent on both. Coverage is the share of the catalogue ever recommended, so higher means a smaller filter bubble. These gains come together with the accuracy gains, because diversity is part of the coalition utility the Shapley weights are computed from, not a re-ranking step.
60: The ablation, per dataset: each row removes one component and reports NDCG at twenty and the drop. Context matters most: minus 8.2 percent on MovieLens-1M and minus 11 percent on Amazon-Book. The hypergraph structure is second, 6.8 and 8.9 percent. Removing the Shapley weighting costs 4.6 and 6.1 percent, more on the sparser data. Diversity and attention follow. Every component contributes, and no single one explains the whole gain.
61: The cost, reported openly. On MovieLens-1M, DyHuCoG trains in about two thousand seconds against eleven hundred for HPCF, roughly 1.78 times. Inference is 1.84 milliseconds per query on MovieLens and 8.52 on Amazon, well within real time. Memory is 4.4 gigabytes against 4.1. On convergence, M equal to fifty gives ninety-nine percent accuracy and one hundred gives 99.5, so fifty is the right operating point.
62: Significance. Paired t-tests on per-user NDCG at twenty over six thousand and forty users, with Holm-Bonferroni correction. Against HPCF the t-statistic is 46.38, Cohen's d is 1.33, and the p-value is of the order of ten to the minus two hundred and seventy; Wilcoxon agrees. The effect size matters: with six thousand users a tiny difference can look significant, so a d above 0.8 shows the gain is real. These tests cover MovieLens-1M; Amazon-Book stays descriptive.
63: DyHuCoG also helps where recommenders are weakest. For users with five or fewer interactions, NDCG at twenty is about ten percent over HPCF; for cold-start items, plus 9.6 percent, and the gain holds on Yelp2018. On interpretability, the SHAP waterfall breaks a recommendation into the same ranking, diversity, context and preference components used in training. And because Shapley measures marginal utility, weak but informative interactions keep their influence, which reduces popularity bias.
64: The answers. RQ3: yes, the Shapley estimates set the hyperedge weights while the model learns. RQ4: yes, ranking, coverage and diversity improve together on both datasets, with the largest gains where data are sparsest. All three objectives are met, with gains over HPCF of 9.8 and 13.3 percent in NDCG, 16 and 30 percent in coverage, and 12 percent in diversity.
65: In short: attribution becomes part of how the recommender learns, the accuracy-diversity trade-off moves, the largest gains are on the sparsest data, and the improvement is statistically large.
66: The limitations, stated honestly. A compute overhead of about 1.78 times HPCF. A dependence on meaningful context. A Monte Carlo estimator that could use variance reduction. An ablation that removes one component at a time, so it does not test combinations. And baselines fixed in early 2026, so I claim superiority only against the tested models.
67: The takeaway is the conceptual shift of the thesis. Attribution is a first-class part of the learning objective, not a post-hoc check, and the explanation is a direct read-out of the objective the model optimises. That makes it faithful by design, and it fits the transparency requirements of new AI regulation. Explanation should be part of the model itself.
68: Let me bring everything together: the synthesis, the publications, the limitations, the perspectives, and the thesis answer. Time check: about minute 36.
69: Three contributions, one thread: explain, scale, guide. C1 explains black-box clustering via Shapley. C2 keeps that explanation consistent at scale and across levels, with Proposition 6.1. C3 carries the same logic inside the learning of a recommender. One cooperative-game definition, three value functions, and the same Shapley logic explains a partition, stays consistent across levels, and guides what a recommender learns.
70: Three journal articles, all as first author. Contribution I with Redwane Nesmaoui, Mohamed Mbarek and Professor Lazaar, in Procedia Computer Science, 2023. Contribution II with Redwane Nesmaoui and Professor Lazaar, in IJACSA, 2025. Contribution III, DyHuCoG, in IJIES, 2026. A related article led by Redwane Nesmaoui applies the same cooperative-game view to real-time contribution adjustment. IJACSA and IJIES are Scopus-indexed.
71: The limitations. On computation, exact Shapley is not feasible, so every contribution relies on approximation or surrogates. On method, the clustering chapters depend on surrogate fidelity and the recommendation results on meaningful context. On experiments, the clustering work is tabular and the recommendation work is offline, with no user study of actionability yet. And on the claim: not one unified framework that removes all tension, but a shared, well-founded view that works across both tasks.
72: Future work turns these limits into an agenda. Scalable attribution: lower-variance estimators and adaptive refresh rules. Online and streaming recommendation, with graphs that keep changing. User-centred evaluation: do these explanations improve analyst judgement, trust and quality of action? And a broader trustworthy-AI evaluation, including fairness, in line with the regulatory requirements I mentioned at the start.
73: To conclude. 9: A quick tour of the approaches we build on. Collaborative filtering works on the idea that similar users will like similar items, computed from the user side or the item side. Content-based filtering recommends items whose features match a profile, and hybrid methods combine both. Matrix factorisation splits the interaction matrix into latent factors: compact and effective, but hidden. Graph-based methods, including LightGCN and hypergraph extensions, pass information over an interaction structure and capture multi-hop or higher-order relations. Each one makes the model stronger, but each one makes interpretation harder in its own way: matrix factorisation hid the meaning of the latent dimensions; graph models left importance implicit; hypergraph models added higher-order relations but assumed all messages matter equally. That equal-messages assumption is one of the things I will challenge.
